title: MATCH Function Exact Match
description: MATCH with match_type 0 is Excel's exact-match lookup. See how MATCH finds a precise position in a range and how to use it safely with INDEX and XMATCH.
intro: MATCH is the small lookup that powers INDEX/MATCH, two-way lookups, and most array tricks behind the scenes. Set match_type to 0 and you get a strict, exact-match position lookup that ignores the sort order of your data. This guide explains the third argument in plain English, shows the difference between MATCH and XMATCH, and builds a robust INDEX/MATCH that does not break when columns move.
prerequisites: Familiarity with cell ranges and arguments

sections.title: MATCH Syntax and the Three Match Types
sections.content: MATCH takes a value, a one-row or one-column range, and a match_type number. 0 means exact match (no sorting required), 1 means 'less than or equal to' on ascending data, and -1 means 'greater than or equal to' on descending data. For exact lookups always use 0; the other two are reserved for range-bucket problems like tax tables.

example.explanation: match_type 0 ignores sort order and returns the relative position of the exact match, or #N/A if it is missing.

tips: MATCH returns a position, not a value. Wrap it in INDEX or use XMATCH on its own.

sections.title: Combining MATCH with INDEX for Lookups
sections.content: INDEX/MATCH is the classic replacement for VLOOKUP that works in any direction and tolerates column inserts. MATCH locates the row (or column), and INDEX pulls the value from there.

example.result: Sales value of the row where column A = 'Apricot'
example.explanation: MATCH returns e.g. 5, so INDEX returns the 5th value of B2:B20, which is the Apricot sales figure.

tips: INDEX/MATCH looks LEFT, something VLOOKUP cannot do (VLOOKUP needs the lookup column on the left).

sections.title: Handling 'Not Found' Cleanly
sections.content: A bare MATCH returns #N/A when the value is missing, which can break downstream formulas. Wrap MATCH in IFERROR (Excel) or wrap INDEX/MATCH together to substitute a friendly default like 'Not found' or 0.

example.result: "Not found" or the matching sales value
example.explanation: If MATCH returns #N/A, IFERROR swaps it for the string 'Not found', keeping reports clean.

tips: In Google Sheets the equivalent is IFNA; in Excel IFNA catches #N/A specifically while IFERROR catches any error.

sections.title: MATCH vs XMATCH (Microsoft 365)
sections.content: XMATCH is the modern replacement for MATCH with clearer match modes and search modes. It defaults to exact match (no third argument required), supports wildcard text, last-item searches, and binary search on sorted data. For new work in Excel 365 or Google Sheets (where XMATCH is also available), prefer XMATCH.

example.explanation: XMATCH without a third argument is exact match and more readable than MATCH(value, range, 0).

tips: Use XMATCH(..., ..., 0, -1) to search from the end and return the LAST match instead of the first.

sections.title: MATCH for Two-Way and Multi-Column Lookups
sections.content: MATCH powers two-dimensional lookups when nested twice: once across the headers and once down the rows. The formula below finds the value at the intersection of a given row label and column header - useful for gradebooks, schedules, and matrix pricing.

example.explanation: The first MATCH picks the row, the second MATCH picks the column, and INDEX returns the cell at that intersection.

tips: Use absolute references (e.g. $A$2:$A$10) when copying the formula so the lookup ranges do not shift.

functionsUsed.name: MATCH
functionsUsed.description: MATCH searches for a specified item in a range and returns its relative position.

functionsUsed.name: INDEX
functionsUsed.description: INDEX returns the value at a specified position in a range or array.

functionsUsed.name: XMATCH
functionsUsed.description: XMATCH returns the relative position of a lookup value within a lookup array, with modern options for match mode (exact, wildcard, next smaller/larger) and search mode (first, last, binary).

functionsUsed.name: VLOOKUP
functionsUsed.description: VLOOKUP (Vertical Lookup) is a built-in function in Excel and Google Sheets that searches for a value in the first column of a table and returns a value in the same row from a specified column.

summary: MATCH with match_type 0 is the simplest exact-match lookup: give it a value, a range, and 0, and it returns the relative position. Pair MATCH with INDEX to look up a value (not just a position), wrap both in IFERROR to handle missing entries, and upgrade to XMATCH when you are on Excel 365 for cleaner syntax and richer search modes.
